title: Work with a wide range of patterns and inverses of functions and solve related problems

lessons.title: Functions and their patterns
lessons.html:
What is a function?

A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. We write y = f(x). The set of allowed inputs is the domain; the set of outputs is the range. Functions describe many farm situations: the cost of fertiliser depends on the number of bags, the growth of a calf depends on its age, and the volume of water in a tank depends on time.

Families of functions

TypeGeneral formGraph shapeFarm example
Lineary = mx + cStraight lineTotal cost = R450 per bag × bags + R300 delivery
Quadraticy = ax² + bx + cParabolaYield response to fertiliser that rises then falls
Hyperbolicy = k/xHyperbolaDays to finish a job = work ÷ number of workers
Exponentialy = a·bˣRapid growth or decay curveGrowth of an unchecked aphid population; value of a depreciating tractor

Effects of parameters

  • In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (rate of change) and c is the y-intercept.
  • In y = ax² + q, a changes the steepness and whether the parabola opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0); q shifts it up or down.
  • In y = k/x + q, k determines which quadrants the graph lies in; q shifts the horizontal asymptote.
  • In y = a·bˣ, b > 1 gives growth, 0 < b < 1 gives decay.

Example

A maize yield trial gives yield Y (t/ha) = −0,0001N² + 0,04N + 3 where N is kg nitrogen per ha. The turning point is at N = −b/(2a) = −0,04 ÷ (−0,0002) = 200 kg/ha, giving Y = −0,0001(40 000) + 8 + 3 = 7 t/ha. Beyond 200 kg/ha, extra nitrogen reduces yield in this model.

lessons.title: Inverse functions
lessons.html:
Working backwards

An inverse function reverses the original function: if f takes x to y, then f⁻¹ takes y back to x. Inverses answer questions like 'how many bags can I buy for R10 000?' when you know the cost function.

Finding an inverse

  1. Write y = f(x).
  2. Swap x and y.
  3. Solve for y.
  4. Write y = f⁻¹(x).

Example (linear): f(x) = 450x + 300. Swap: x = 450y + 300. Solve: y = (x − 300) ÷ 450. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 300)/450. With R10 000: (10 000 − 300) ÷ 450 ≈ 21,6, so 21 full bags.

Inverse of a quadratic

For f(x) = 2x², swapping gives x = 2y², so y = ±√(x/2). This is not a function because one input gives two outputs. To make the inverse a function, restrict the domain of the original, for example x ≥ 0, giving f⁻¹(x) = √(x/2).

Exponential and logarithmic functions

The inverse of y = bˣ is the logarithmic function y = log_b x. For example, the inverse of y = 10ˣ is y = log x.

Example: a tractor bought for R800 000 loses 15% of its value each year: V = 800 000 × 0,85ᵗ. When will it be worth R400 000? 0,85ᵗ = 0,5, so t = log 0,5 ÷ log 0,85 ≈ 4,3 years.

Graphs of inverses

The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x. The domain of f becomes the range of f⁻¹ and vice versa.

Testing whether an inverse is a function

Use the horizontal line test on the original graph: if any horizontal line cuts the graph more than once, the inverse is not a function unless the domain is restricted.

lessons.title: Solving problems with functions and inverses
lessons.html:
Applying functions

Problem-solving approach

  1. Read the situation and identify the variables.
  2. Decide which family of function fits the pattern (constant rate, turning point, inverse proportion, percentage growth).
  3. Find the parameters from the information or data.
  4. Use the function, or its inverse, to answer the question.
  5. Check the answer makes sense in context, including domain limits.

Example 1: inverse proportion

Six workers take 10 days to pick an orchard. Days D = 60 ÷ W, where W is the number of workers. To finish in 4 days: W = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 workers. Here the function is its own inverse form: W = 60/D.

Example 2: exponential growth

An aphid population doubles every 3 days from 200 per plant: P = 200 × 2^(t/3). When will it reach 3 200? 2^(t/3) = 16 = 2⁴, so t/3 = 4 and t = 12 days. This shows why early scouting matters.

Example 3: reading graphs

From a graph of feed cost against kilograms, identify the gradient (cost per kg) and intercept (fixed delivery cost). Use the inverse to find how many kilograms a given budget buys.

Number patterns

Patterns are functions with whole-number inputs. A linear pattern has a constant first difference (e.g. 5; 8; 11; 14: rule Tₙ = 3n + 2). A quadratic pattern has a constant second difference (e.g. 2; 6; 12; 20: first differences 4; 6; 8, second difference 2, rule Tₙ = n² + n).

Key points

  • A function gives exactly one output for each input.
  • Recognise linear, quadratic, hyperbolic and exponential patterns and their parameters.
  • Find an inverse by swapping x and y and solving for y.
  • The inverse graph is a reflection in y = x; restrict domains where needed.
  • Logarithms are inverses of exponential functions and solve growth and decay problems.
